lesson.title: Layered Architecture: Dividing an Impossible Job into Manageable Pieces
lesson.summary: Layered architecture organizes networking into a stack of independent layers, each solving one problem and relying on encapsulation to hand data to the layer below it.
lesson.body:
Getting a message from one program on one computer to another program on a different computer, possibly on the other side of the planet, requires solving many distinct problems at once: how to represent bits as electrical or optical signals, how to address a specific machine on a specific network, how to make sure data arrives in order and without loss, and how to interpret the actual content once it arrives. Trying to solve all of these problems in one single, tangled piece of software would be difficult to build and nearly impossible to fix or improve. Layered architecture is the design strategy that avoids this by splitting the overall job into a stack of layers, each responsible for exactly one of these problems.

Each layer in the stack offers a defined service to the layer above it, and to do so, it communicates with its counterpart layer on the receiving computer using an agreed set of rules, which is precisely what a protocol is. A layer does not need to know how the layer below it actually works, only that it can hand data down and trust it will eventually arrive at the matching layer on the other end. This reliance on well defined protocols between layers is what makes it possible to change how one layer works, for example replacing Wi-Fi with a wired Ethernet connection, without having to rewrite anything in the layers above it.

Encapsulation is the specific mechanism that makes this layering work in practice rather than remaining just a conceptual diagram. As covered earlier, each layer takes the data handed to it, wraps it with its own header, and passes the result down as payload for the next layer. On the receiving side, decapsulation reverses this, each layer stripping its own header before handing the remainder upward. Without encapsulation, there would be no way to actually keep each layer's control information separate from every other layer's control information within a single stream of bytes.

Consider ordinary web browsing as a worked example of why this division of labor helps. The application layer only has to worry about the content of an HTTP request. The transport layer only has to worry about making sure that request's bytes arrive reliably and in order, using port numbers to route them to the correct program. The network layer only has to worry about getting a packet from the sending network to the receiving network, using IP addresses. The link and physical layers only have to worry about actually moving bits across one specific physical connection, using hardware addresses and electrical or optical signaling. No single piece of software has to hold all of these concerns in its head at once.

This same idea of dividing responsibilities into layers, connected by protocols and glued together by encapsulation and decapsulation, has been formalized into two widely referenced models, the OSI reference model and the TCP IP model, which the next two chapters describe in detail.
